title: Voters left off draft rolls in Delhi and six states get fresh chance, without Form 6
dek: Excluded electors in seven states will get fresh enumeration forms and keep their voter ID numbers. Bengal is not covered.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Election Commission of India has given voters who were left out of the draft electoral rolls in seven states and Union Territories a fresh chance to be included in the final rolls, without having to apply as new voters. The move covers Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland. West Bengal is not among them.

In a three-page letter to the chief electoral officers of those states, dated 6 November, the Commission directed them to issue fresh enumeration forms to electors who were marked "ASDD" (absent, shifted, dead or duplicate) during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) because they had not returned the forms they were given, according to reports of the letter. The Congress called it a "belated admission of wrongful deletion", according to reports; the Commission has defended the revision, pointing to the Supreme Court's scrutiny of it.

## What the letter says

Booth-level officers are to try to reach the excluded electors through house-to-house visits, WhatsApp, email and text messages, according to reports of the letter. Booth-wise lists of those left out, with the likely reason for exclusion, are to be displayed at polling stations and local government offices and uploaded to the chief electoral officers' websites.

Electors who still live at the same address can submit the enumeration form with a written statement explaining why they did not return it earlier. Those who have moved within the same state do not need to file Form 8, the usual form for a change of address; they can submit the enumeration form with a statement giving the new address and constituency, and proof of residence. For homeless electors with no address documents, the booth-level officer's field verification report will count as proof of residence. People who have already filed Form 6, the application for new voters, during the revision need not file again.

Those who are restored will keep their existing voter ID (EPIC) numbers, rather than registering as first-time voters. Each application will be examined by the Electoral Registration Officer under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, so inclusion is not automatic. Reports of the letter did not give a deadline for applications or a date for the final rolls.

## Why it matters

The change reverses the Commission's earlier position that voters left out of the draft rolls had to apply afresh on Form 6 whether or not they had voted before. At a hearing on 28 October, the Supreme Court questioned that approach. Transparency activists Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, who have challenged exclusions in Delhi in the Supreme Court, said in a joint statement that they welcomed the communication and called it "an important step in addressing large scale exclusions caused during SIR". They said that of 47.56 lakh names deleted in Delhi and placed on the ASDD list in the first phase, 31.59 lakh were marked as permanently shifted and 11.73 lakh as absent or untraceable.

In Maharashtra, a petition before the Supreme Court says nearly 3 crore names were removed, including about 1.22 crore under a "logical discrepancy" category; the court sought responses from the Commission but declined to stay publication of the revised rolls, according to reports.

## The political fight

The SIR, a door-to-door re-verification of every elector, has become one of the sharpest disputes in national politics. The Congress and other opposition parties accuse the Commission of removing eligible voters at the behest of the BJP, which the Commission and the BJP deny. On Thursday Union Home Minister Amit Shah offered a special session of Parliament to debate the SIR if the Congress wrote to the Prime Minister, while Rahul Gandhi has continued to attack the exercise. Reports this week also said that two election commissioners had recorded objections to some decisions on the revision; the Commission said all major decisions were unanimous.

In Bengal, which is not covered by the new letter, the dispute has centred on appeals against names restored to the rolls, according to reports.

## What happens next

Chief electoral officers in the seven states must now issue the forms and publish the lists of excluded electors. The Supreme Court is still hearing petitions on exclusions in Delhi and Maharashtra.
